transcript:
Meeting Header:
Date: 2026-07-08 16:00 UTC
Duration: 42 minutes
Attendees: Emily Zhang (Redwood AE), Miguel Torres (Redwood SE), Alice Monroe (Zephyr CTO), Tom Rhee (Zephyr SRE), Jamal Ortiz (Zephyr ML Eng)

Summary (auto): Quick discovery to understand Zephyr's latency SLOs and benchmarking needs for inference. Agreed to run comparative benchmarks and share pricing + security docs.

[00:00:00] Emily (AE): hey everyone, thanks for joining, we set aside about 45 minutes for this, i'll let miguel and i run through a few questions and then dig into the latency/throughput stuff you sent over in the form.
[00:00:12] Alice (Zephyr): yep thanks, we've been excited to talk. main ask is we need to understand if redwood can hit our p95 targets on small streaming responses and also what throughput we can expect when we scale up concurrency.
[00:00:25] Miguel (SE): great, high level question first — are you leaning hosted, dedicated, or private? that changes how we think about tail latencies and capacity planning.
[00:00:35] Tom (Zephyr): leaning dedicated for prod for data isolation, but we'll probably prototype on hosted. we want SLA-ish guarantees for p95.
[00:00:44] Emily: got it. what p95 are you targeting and for what request sizes?
[00:00:48] Jamal (Zephyr): for our chat UI: most prompts are short, ~30-60 tokens in, 100-250 tokens out. p95 target around 200-400ms for streaming first-byte and continuous streaming; for non-streamed completions maybe 300-500ms p95.
[00:01:06] Miguel: ok that's helpful. couple of clarifying questions on concurrency — when you say 50-200 concurrent users is that concurrent websocket streams or concurrent requests?
[00:01:15] Tom: websocket streams, persistent connections. concurrency profile is spiky; we have daily peaks where 300-400 users are active but sustained 70-120.
[00:01:26] Miguel: perfect. for streaming workloads our metrics break latency into first-byte and tail; first-byte is generally where you see model startup and token generation latency. with hosted we have multi-tenant pools which are fast but tail can vary, dedicated gives much more predictable p95 because you control GPU pools.
[00:01:42] Alice: can you ballpark tokens/sec and tokens/sec per GPU for the model types? we're considering a 7B dense model first then maybe a quantized 13B variant.
[00:01:52] Miguel: ballpark depends on hardware and quantization — on an H100-like instance with optimized kernels a 7B can do 1500-2500 tokens/sec for batched non-streaming at moderate sequence lengths, streaming lower per-stream but aggregated higher. for 13B quantized we might see 600-1200 tokens/sec per GPU. with batching and continuous kv cache you can push aggregate throughput up.
[00:02:12] Tom: and for p95, what does that translate to?
[00:02:15] Miguel: if you have many concurrent streams and limited batching opportunity, p95 is influenced by scheduling and preemption. dedicated pools reduce noisy neighbors — we've seen p95s in the 150-350ms range for short streaming frames on dedicated for 7B models, hosted is more like 250-600ms depending on load. caveat: those are approximate and depend on prompt length, tokenizer, and output size.
[00:02:36] Emily: also worth calling out caching — prefix/KV cache is big: if you have repeated context or persistent sessions we can cache kv to avoid re-compute for previous tokens which helps p95.
[00:02:45] Jamal: our chat history is short, but user context is reused a lot across turns, so KV caching sounds useful. if we move to private on-prem it's more about network and infra predictability.
[00:02:56] [00:03:00] Speaker 5: (inaudible)
[00:03:05] Alice: security is a hard constraint — SOC2 is must, KMS integration for keys and audit logs, and SSO. can you confirm redwood's capabilities?
[00:03:13] Emily: yes we're SOC2, we have KMS integrations and audit logs; for private deployments we can support customer-managed KMS and VPC peering or on-prem options. we'll send the SOC2 cert and KMS integration doc.
[00:03:25] Tom: ok good. on the bench plan — we'd like to run a tokens/sec and p95 benchmark comparing hosted vs dedicated vs our on-prem when we spin a private env. what does redwood need from us to run that?
[00:03:37] Miguel: we typically ask for: a representative prompt set (small/med/large), concurrency profile (percentiles, spikes), model choices and desired quant profiles, and a target hardware list if you have preferences. we'll run a baseline on hosted, then on a dedicated pool sized to your concurrency, capture p50/p95/p99, tokens/sec, and CPU/GPU util traces.
[00:03:58] Jamal: we can share prompts and a week of usage logs to shape the concurrency profile. can you run streaming-targeted tests, i.e., first-byte latency and per-frame latencies?
[00:04:07] Miguel: absolutely. we'll include streaming-first-byte and per-token intervals in the test harness, and we can output a CSV with timestamps to compute p95.
[00:04:15] Alice: curious about graceful degradation — if you hit capacity spikes can you fallback to a cheaper quantized model or degrade features to keep latency?
[00:04:23] Miguel: yes, smart routing can fallback to lower-cost quantized variants or route to other regions; dedicated pools can have burst capacity to hosted tier. we also have canary/A-B rollout features. there are tradeoffs with quality.
[00:04:33] Tom: how about autoscaling — if we use dedicated, can it handle a sudden 3x spike without huge pre-warm?
[00:04:38] Miguel: autoscaling is configurable; for GPU-backed inference warm-up matters. we recommend reserved baseline capacity to hit p95 targets and burst policies to absorb short spikes; for sustained spikes add more capacity. we'll size pools based on your sustained concurrent stream target and target p95.
[00:04:52] Emily: quick question on metrics — what observability will you need? we provide per-route latency histograms, token-level cost breakdown, and tracing hooks so you can correlate with app traces.
[00:05:01] Jamal: perfect. can you also capture per-request model variant and quantization used? we want to track any quality regressions tied to model switches.
[00:05:07] Miguel: yes that's in our standard telemetry.
[00:05:10] Alice: for the benchmark, what's your recommended p95 target thresholds to be confident in production for our use case?
[00:05:16] Miguel: for short streaming messages, aim for p95 first-byte under 300ms on dedicated for a good UX; for non-streamed completions p95 under 400ms is reasonable. if you require sub-200ms p95 at scale that usually requires more aggressive hardware (H100) and reserved capacity.
[00:05:33] Tom: if we go H100 dedicated and quant 4-bit for 13B, do you have estimates?
[00:05:38] Miguel: a 13B 4-bit quant on H100 we might see 700-1200 tokens/sec aggregate and p95 streaming first-byte in the 200-350ms range depending on concurrency and batching. again this is approximate.
[00:05:52] Alice: do you support local on-prem inference with your private product? network latency will likely be lower but ops overhead is a concern.
[00:05:58] Emily: yes our Private deployment can be on-prem or in-customer VPC, with control plane options. ops overhead is higher but gives you full control and predictable latency if your network/hardware is stable.
[00:06:08] Jamal: ok let's talk numbers — our target steady concurrent streams is 120 with peaks to 350. we want to start with 7B then evaluate 13B quant. what's rough sizing?
[00:06:16] Miguel: rough rule of thumb: depending on batching, a single GPU can handle many concurrent streams if each stream produces tokens slowly; if each stream needs low-latency token-by-token streaming, you need more GPU capacity. for 120 steady streams on 7B, a dedicated pool of 2-4 high-end GPUs (H100 or A100) might be enough, but we'll do exact sizing in the benchmark.
[00:06:32] Tom: and for cost — can you send cost per token and per-hour for dedicated nodes?
[00:06:37] Emily: yes we'll include detailed cost model in the pricing doc.
[00:06:41] Alice: any known issues with websocket streaming at scale? we've seen connection churn impact token pacing elsewhere.
[00:06:47] Miguel: connection churn can cause cache misses and reloading; we recommend sticky routing and session affinity to preserve KV cache and maintain lower tail latency. also batching across streams is limited for websockets but we have continuous batching and adaptive schedulers that help.
[00:07:02] Jamal: on the benchmark harness, will you simulate realistic client pacing and jitter?
[00:07:06] Miguel: yes we can simulate jitter and real-world pacing; we also capture per-token timestamps so you can compute effective tokens/sec and per-frame p95.
[00:07:12] Emily: let's capture a proposed benchmark plan on the call: 1) Zephyr sends prompt set + concurrency profile 2) Redwood runs hosted baseline 3) Redwood runs dedicated pool sized to target 4) Redwood shares raw traces + summary and recommendations.
[00:07:24] Alice: agreed. timeline?
[00:07:26] Emily: we can turn around hosted tests in 3-5 business days after we get prompts; dedicated bench depends on pool provisioning but target 7-10 days.
[00:07:34] Tom: that's fine.
[00:07:36] Jamal: one more question on quantization — do you support mixed precision and QLoRA-style finetune quant or just native quantized variants?
[00:07:44] Miguel: we support multiple quant profiles and can run evals on quantized artifacts; for finetune-quant combos we'd validate accuracy and perf in the benchmark.
[00:07:52] Alice: competitors — we've looked at OpenAI and Anthropic for hosted and did a POC with vertex custom infra; any differences to flag?
[00:07:59] Miguel: main diffs: OpenAI/Anthropic are managed models with limits on private deployments; Vertex/Cloud vendors give infra control but not necessarily inference-optimized runtime; Redwood aims to combine runtime optimizations, predictable costs, and private deployment options. we'll include a short comparison doc.
[00:08:15] Speaker 5: (crosstalk)
[00:08:18] Emily: ok, recap and next steps: we'll send pricing + SOC2/KMS docs, miguel will prep benchmark harness and run hosted + dedicated baseline once we have prompts, and zephyr will share prompt set and usage profile.
[00:08:30] Tom: action — we'll share the prompt set and logs by friday.
[00:08:34] Emily: perfect. any final Qs?
[00:08:36] Alice: none from me, thanks.
[00:08:38] Jamal: thanks both.
[00:08:40] Miguel: thanks everyone, we'll follow up with the plan.

(End of recording)
